title: SQL Reference
description: A compact reference of the SQL statements, clauses, operators and functions covered in the tutorial, grouped by purpose, with syntax, a short example and the lesson that explains each one.

entries.name: SELECT
entries.summary: Reads rows from a table and returns the listed columns or expressions; * means every column.

example.code: SELECT name, price FROM products;

notes: Columns appear in the order listed
Prefer explicit columns over * in application code

entries.name: SELECT DISTINCT
entries.summary: Removes duplicate rows from the result; with several columns, keeps each distinct combination.

example.code: SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers;

entries.name: AS (alias)
entries.summary: Renames a result column or a table for the duration of the query; names with spaces need double quotes.

example.code: SELECT price * 1.2 AS price_with_tax FROM products AS p;

notes: The keyword AS is optional in most databases but improves readability

entries.name: FROM
entries.summary: Names the table (or tables, views and subqueries) the query reads from.

entries.name: WHERE
entries.summary: Keeps only the rows for which the condition is true; runs before grouping and aggregation.

example.code: SELECT name FROM products WHERE price > 10 AND category = 'Office';

notes: Comparisons with NULL are never true; use IS NULL
AND binds tighter than OR; add parentheses

entries.name: ORDER BY
entries.summary: Sorts the result by one or more columns or expressions, ascending by default or descending with DESC.
entries.syntax: ORDER BY column [ASC | DESC], column2 [ASC | DESC]

example.code: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY category, price DESC;

notes: Without ORDER BY the row order is undefined
NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST is available in SQLite 3.30+, PostgreSQL and Oracle

entries.name: LIMIT and OFFSET
entries.summary: Returns at most n rows, optionally skipping the first m rows, for top-N queries and pagination.

example.code: SELECT name FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2;

notes: SQL Server uses TOP n or OFFSET ... FETCH; the standard form is FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY
Always combine with ORDER BY

entries.summary: Compare two values; <> (or !=) means not equal. Text and ISO dates compare alphabetically.

example.code: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE joined >= '2025-01-01';

entries.name: AND, OR, NOT
entries.summary: Combine or negate conditions. AND is evaluated before OR, so use parentheses when mixing them.
entries.syntax: condition AND condition | condition OR condition | NOT condition

example.code: WHERE (category = 'Office' OR category = 'Stationery') AND price < 10

entries.name: LIKE
entries.summary: Matches text against a pattern: % stands for any sequence of characters and _ for exactly one.

example.code: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE 'G%';

notes: Case-insensitive for ASCII letters in SQLite, collation-dependent (usually case-insensitive) in MySQL, case-sensitive in PostgreSQL (use ILIKE)

entries.name: IN
entries.summary: True when the value appears in a list of values or in the result of a subquery.

example.code: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE country IN ('US', 'UK');

notes: NOT IN returns nothing if the list contains a NULL; prefer NOT EXISTS

entries.name: BETWEEN
entries.summary: Tests an inclusive range; both boundary values match.

example.code: SELECT name FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 5 AND 40;

entries.name: IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
entries.summary: The only correct tests for a missing value; = NULL never matches anything.
entries.syntax: column IS NULL | column IS NOT NULL

example.code: SELECT title FROM tickets WHERE assignee IS NULL;

entries.name: || (concatenation)
entries.summary: Joins text values into one string in standard SQL, SQLite and PostgreSQL; MySQL and SQL Server use CONCAT().

example.code: SELECT name || ' (' || country || ')' AS label FROM customers;

notes: Any NULL operand makes the whole result NULL; wrap with COALESCE

entries.name: INSERT INTO ... VALUES
entries.summary: Adds one or more rows; omitted columns receive their default, NULL, or an auto-generated id.
entries.syntax: INSERT INTO table (col1, col2) VALUES (v1, v2), (v3, v4);

example.code: INSERT INTO products (name, category, price) VALUES ('Desk lamp', 'Office', 24.90);

notes: Double a single quote inside text: 'O''Brien'
Always list the columns

entries.name: INSERT INTO ... SELECT
entries.summary: Inserts every row returned by a query, for copying, archiving or seeding tables.
entries.syntax: INSERT INTO target (cols) SELECT cols FROM source WHERE ...;

example.code: INSERT INTO archived_orders SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ordered_on < '2025-03-01';

entries.name: UPDATE
entries.summary: Changes columns of the rows selected by WHERE; without WHERE every row changes.
entries.syntax: UPDATE table SET col1 = value1, col2 = value2 WHERE condition;

example.code: UPDATE products SET price = ROUND(price * 1.1, 2) WHERE category = 'Stationery';

notes: Run the same WHERE as a SELECT first
Expressions may refer to the current value

entries.name: DELETE
entries.summary: Removes the rows selected by WHERE; without WHERE the table is emptied.

example.code: DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 8;

notes: SQLite's changes() returns the number of affected rows
TRUNCATE TABLE exists in PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server, not in SQLite

entries.name: RETURNING
entries.summary: Returns columns of the inserted, updated or deleted rows, such as a generated id, in the same statement.

example.code: INSERT INTO products (name, category, price) VALUES ('Webcam', 'Electronics', 45) RETURNING id;

notes: PostgreSQL, SQLite 3.35+ and MariaDB; MySQL uses LAST_INSERT_ID(), SQL Server uses OUTPUT

entries.name: CREATE TABLE
entries.summary: Defines a new table with named, typed columns and optional constraints.
notes: IF NOT EXISTS skips the statement when the table already exists

entries.name: Data types
entries.summary: SQLite uses INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB and NUMERIC with flexible type affinity; PostgreSQL and MySQL enforce declared types such as INT, DECIMAL(p,s), VARCHAR(n), DATE and BOOLEAN.
notes: Store money as DECIMAL/NUMERIC or integer cents, never as floating point
SQLite stores dates as ISO 8601 text and booleans as 0/1
SQLite STRICT tables (3.37+) enforce declared types

entries.name: PRIMARY KEY
entries.summary: Uniquely identifies each row; implies NOT NULL and UNIQUE. Several columns form a composite key.
entries.syntax: id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY | PRIMARY KEY (col1, col2)

entries.name: Auto-generated ids
entries.summary: SQLite auto-numbers an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column; AUTOINCREMENT prevents reuse of deleted ids. Other databases use IDENTITY, SERIAL or AUTO_INCREMENT.
notes: PostgreSQL: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY
MySQL: INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY
SQL Server: INT IDENTITY(1,1)

entries.name: NOT NULL and DEFAULT
entries.summary: NOT NULL requires a value for the column; DEFAULT supplies one when an insert omits it.
entries.syntax: col type NOT NULL DEFAULT value

example.code: remote INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0

entries.name: UNIQUE
entries.summary: Rejects a second row with the same value in the column (or combination of columns).

example.code: email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE

notes: Creates an index automatically

entries.name: CHECK
entries.summary: Requires a condition to be true for every row, such as a non-negative balance or a limited set of statuses.

example.code: balance REAL NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance >= 0)

entries.name: FOREIGN KEY / REFERENCES
entries.summary: Requires the column to hold a value that exists in another table's key; ON DELETE chooses what happens to child rows.
entries.syntax: col INTEGER REFERENCES parent(id) [ON DELETE CASCADE | SET NULL | RESTRICT]

example.code: team_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES teams(id) ON DELETE CASCADE

notes: SQLite enforces it only after PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON
PostgreSQL always enforces; MySQL with InnoDB

entries.name: ALTER TABLE
entries.summary: Changes an existing table: add, rename or drop a column, or rename the table.
entries.syntax: ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN col type; ALTER TABLE t RENAME COLUMN a TO b; ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN col;

example.code: ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN stock INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

notes: SQLite cannot add or drop constraints with ALTER TABLE; rebuild the table instead

entries.name: DROP TABLE
entries.summary: Deletes a table together with all of its rows and indexes; IF EXISTS avoids an error when it is missing.

example.code: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS temp_list;

entries.name: JOIN (INNER JOIN)
entries.summary: Pairs rows of two tables whose ON condition matches; rows without a partner are left out.
entries.syntax: FROM a JOIN b ON b.col = a.col
notes: Without ON every row is paired with every row (cross product)

entries.name: LEFT JOIN
entries.summary: Keeps every row of the left table and fills the right table's columns with NULL when nothing matches.
entries.syntax: FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.col = a.col

example.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

notes: A WHERE condition on the right table turns it back into an inner join
RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN exist in SQLite 3.39+ and PostgreSQL; MySQL lacks FULL JOIN

entries.name: Self join
entries.summary: Joins a table with itself using two aliases, for example to pair rows that share a value.
entries.syntax: FROM t a JOIN t b ON a.col = b.col AND a.id < b.id

entries.name: GROUP BY
entries.summary: Forms one group per distinct value (or expression) and computes aggregates per group.
entries.syntax: SELECT col, aggregate(...) FROM table GROUP BY col

example.code: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS products FROM products GROUP BY category;

notes: Select only grouped columns and aggregates; other columns have no defined value

entries.name: HAVING
entries.summary: Filters groups after aggregation, which WHERE cannot do.

example.code: SELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY country HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

entries.name: Subquery
entries.summary: A SELECT nested inside another statement: as a single value, as a list for IN, or as a derived table in FROM.
entries.syntax: WHERE col > (SELECT ...) | WHERE col IN (SELECT ...) | FROM (SELECT ...) AS alias

example.code: SELECT name FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);

notes: A scalar subquery returning several rows errors in PostgreSQL and MySQL; SQLite uses the first row

entries.name: EXISTS / NOT EXISTS
entries.summary: True when the correlated subquery returns at least one row; safe with NULLs, unlike NOT IN.
entries.syntax: WHERE [NOT] EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE t.col = outer.col)

example.code:
SELECT p.name FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.product_id = p.id);

entries.name: WITH (common table expression)
entries.summary: Names a subquery so the main query can use it like a table, possibly several times; WITH RECURSIVE handles hierarchies.
entries.syntax: WITH name AS (SELECT ...) SELECT ... FROM name;

entries.name: COUNT
entries.summary: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values and COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts different values.

example.code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS buyers FROM orders;

entries.name: SUM and AVG
entries.summary: Total and arithmetic mean of a column or expression, skipping NULL values; AVG always returns a floating-point number.

example.code: SELECT SUM(quantity) AS items, ROUND(AVG(quantity), 2) AS avg_items FROM orders;

entries.name: MIN and MAX
entries.summary: Smallest and largest value of a column (numbers, text or dates). With several arguments, SQLite compares values within one row.

example.code: SELECT MIN(price), MAX(price) FROM products;

notes: Row-wise comparison is GREATEST/LEAST in PostgreSQL and MySQL

entries.name: ROUND, ABS, %
entries.summary: ROUND(x, n) rounds to n decimals, ABS removes the sign and % returns the remainder of an integer division.

example.code: SELECT ROUND(8.99 * 3, 2), ABS(-7), 17 % 5;

notes: Integer / integer is integer division in SQLite, PostgreSQL and SQL Server
MOD(a, b) in PostgreSQL and MySQL

entries.name: UPPER, LOWER, LENGTH
entries.summary: Change the case of text or count its characters.

example.code: SELECT UPPER(name), LENGTH(name) FROM customers;

notes: MySQL uses CHAR_LENGTH for characters; LENGTH counts bytes there

entries.name: SUBSTR, INSTR, TRIM, REPLACE
entries.summary: Extract part of a string, find a position, strip surrounding spaces or replace text.
entries.syntax: SUBSTR(s, start, length) | INSTR(s, 'x') | TRIM(s) | REPLACE(s, 'old', 'new')

example.code: SELECT SUBSTR(name, 1, 3), REPLACE(joined, '-', '/') FROM customers;

notes: Positions count from 1
PostgreSQL and MySQL spell it SUBSTRING; position is POSITION / LOCATE

entries.name: COALESCE / IFNULL
entries.summary: Returns the first non-NULL argument, the standard way to substitute a default for missing data.

example.code: SELECT COALESCE(assignee, 'unassigned') FROM tickets;

notes: IFNULL (SQLite, MySQL) and ISNULL (SQL Server) take exactly two arguments

entries.name: CASE
entries.summary: Returns one of several values depending on conditions, like an if/else chain inside a query.
entries.syntax: CASE WHEN condition THEN value [WHEN ...] ELSE value END

example.code: SELECT name, CASE WHEN price >= 50 THEN 'premium' ELSE 'standard' END AS tier FROM products;

entries.name: date(), datetime(), julianday()
entries.summary: SQLite date functions that parse ISO 8601 text, apply modifiers such as '+1 year', and convert dates to day numbers for arithmetic.

example.code: SELECT date(joined, '+1 year'), julianday('2025-05-05') - julianday('2025-01-15') FROM customers;

notes: Only ISO formats are understood; date('15/01/2025') is NULL
PostgreSQL uses INTERVAL arithmetic, MySQL DATE_ADD and DATEDIFF

entries.name: strftime()
entries.summary: Formats a date or time with C-style codes such as %Y, %m, %d; useful for extracting the year or month.

example.code: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', ordered_on) AS month, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY month;

notes: PostgreSQL: TO_CHAR and EXTRACT; MySQL: DATE_FORMAT and YEAR()

entries.name: CAST and typeof()
entries.summary: CAST converts a value to another type; SQLite's typeof() reports the storage class actually used.
entries.syntax: CAST(expr AS INTEGER | REAL | TEXT) | typeof(expr)

example.code: SELECT CAST('42' AS INTEGER) + 1, typeof(4.5), 7 / CAST(2 AS REAL);

entries.name: CREATE VIEW
entries.summary: Stores a query under a name so it can be used like a table; the query runs again on every access.
entries.syntax: CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ...; DROP VIEW name;

example.code:
CREATE VIEW cheap_products AS
SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price < 10;

notes: SQLite views are read-only; materialized views exist in PostgreSQL and Oracle

entries.name: CREATE INDEX
entries.summary: Builds a sorted structure on one or more columns so lookups, joins and sorts on them avoid a full scan; UNIQUE enforces uniqueness.
entries.syntax: CREATE [UNIQUE] INDEX name ON table (col1, col2); DROP INDEX name;

example.code: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);

notes: Every write must maintain the index
A function applied to the column in WHERE prevents index use

entries.name: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
entries.summary: Shows how SQLite will execute a statement: SCAN reads the whole table, SEARCH ... USING INDEX uses an index.

example.code: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 2;

notes: PostgreSQL and MySQL use EXPLAIN

entries.name: BEGIN and COMMIT
entries.summary: BEGIN starts a transaction in which changes are provisional; COMMIT makes them permanent together.
notes: MySQL also accepts START TRANSACTION
Outside a transaction every statement autocommits

entries.name: ROLLBACK
entries.summary: Discards every change made since BEGIN (or since a savepoint) and ends the transaction.

entries.name: SAVEPOINT
entries.summary: Marks a point inside a transaction so that ROLLBACK TO can undo only the statements after it.
entries.syntax: SAVEPOINT name; ... ROLLBACK TO name; RELEASE name;

entries.name: PRAGMA foreign_keys
entries.summary: SQLite setting that turns foreign key enforcement on for the current connection; off by default.

example.code:
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product_id, quantity, ordered_on) VALUES (99, 1, 1, '2025-09-01');

notes: Must be set on every new connection; put it first in playground scripts
